display_math_plan: $$\int_{a}^{b} x(\tau)\,\delta(\tau-t_0)d\tau = \begin{cases}x(t_0), & a\le t_0\le b \ 0, & t_0<a \text{ or } t_0>b\end{cases}$$

sections.section_title: Introduction to Unit Step as the Integral of an Impulse
sections.learning_goal: Establish that integrating a unit impulse from $-\infty$ to $t$ produces a unit-step switch in the accumulated area and map that rule to $\int_{-\infty}^{t} \delta(\tau) \, d\tau = u(t)$ and $\frac{d}{dt}u(t)=\delta(t)$.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; this is a pure notation-to-symbolic mapping step.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Use the accumulation viewpoint to convert impulse support crossing a moving time upper bound into a binary switch value.

paragraph_plan: Introduce what is being accumulated: total signed area of a unit impulse as the upper limit $t$ sweeps rightward.

example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show the integral is 0 when $t<0$ and 1 when $t \ge 0$, then rewrite compactly as $u(t)$.

sections.section_title: Accumulating a Shifted Unit Impulse
sections.learning_goal: Convert a shifted impulse accumulation into a shifted step by recognizing the shifted include point.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; decision remains algebraic and supports direct step conversion.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Compute $\int_{-\infty}^{t}\delta(\tau-t_0)\,d\tau$ and pick the correct shifted step expression.
distractor_plan: Use wrong shift direction such as $u(t+t_0)$.
Drop the shift and return $u(t)$.
Swap inclusion criterion to $t<t_0$.
Return $\delta(t-t_0)$ instead of the accumulated step.
Give a piecewise interval with incorrect boundary or sign.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Find $\int_{-\infty}^{t}\delta(\tau-3)\,d\tau$ and express the result as a unit step.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Derive $0$ before $t=3$, $1$ at/after $3$, and compact form $u(t-3)$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Extends the baseline by adding a time shift and preserving the same inclusion logic.
solution_step_plan: Shift the impulse center from 0 to $t_0=3$.
practice_variation_axes: Vary the shift parameter in question stems (positive, negative, nonzero values) while keeping the same solution pattern.
Vary notation form requested: piecewise, shifted step, or evaluated-at-point interpretation.

sections.section_title: Deciding Whether the Impulse Has Been Included
sections.learning_goal: Practice the inclusion test for accumulated impulse terms by determining whether integration has crossed the impulse location before moving to the next step.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No graph required if the writer phrases questions as upper-limit checks on shifted support points.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $\int_{-\infty}^{t}\delta(\tau-a)\,d\tau$, determine whether the impulse is included when $t=$ specified values and return the expression.
distractor_plan: Confuse inclusion boundary as strict inequality in all options.
Use an incorrect dependence on sign of $a$.
Choose a constant non-step value instead of a switch.
Swap $t$ and $a$ in the result as $u(a-t)$.
Return scaled constants without accounting for the unscaled unit area.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Decide if the impulse at $\tau=2$ has been accumulated in $\int_{-\infty}^{t}\delta(\tau-2)\,d\tau$ for $t=-1,2,5$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show inclusion is determined by comparing $t$ to the shift point and list the step form that matches the result set.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds the boundary-check test on specific $t$ samples to strengthen the core inclusion criterion before scaling.
solution_step_plan: Compute whether each $t$ value is less than, equal to, or greater than 2.
State that inclusion switches at $t=2$, so the integral equals $u(t-2)$.
practice_variation_axes: Use different sample $t$ values and different shift points while keeping single-step inclusion logic.
Ask for direct value at a point and full step-form form as dual but equivalent responses.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this section as a controlled transition from pure formula recall to inclusion reasoning. Emphasize why this decision is the gate to conversion.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; carry-through of scale factor is captured algebraically in worked examples and questions.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Convert $\int_{-\infty}^{t} 5\delta(\tau+1)\,d\tau$ and identify the output expression.
distractor_plan: Drop the scale factor and use $u(t+1)$.
Multiply by wrong shift or opposite sign in the shift term.
Return $5\delta(t+1)$ instead of an integral-derived step.
Reverse the boundary condition for the shifted step.
Use $5u(1-t)$ instead of $5u(t+1)$.

example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Carry the coefficient through accumulation to produce $5u(t+1)$ with correct boundary handling.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds one controlled wrinkle—magnitude scaling—while reusing the same inclusion logic.
solution_step_plan: Recognize linearity: constant multiplier 5 remains outside the accumulation rule.
Apply inclusion test for shifted impulse at $\tau=-1$.

Vary requested final form between piecewise and $a u(\cdot)$ form.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Unit Impulse as the Derivative of a Unit Step
sections.learning_goal: Establish the identity between differentiating a step transition and obtaining a unit impulse, then connect that identity to shifted and scaled examples.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No visual needed; all reasoning is symbolic.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show that differentiating $u(t)$ produces $\delta(t)$ and that differentiation preserves shifts and scales: $\frac{d}{dt}[A\,u(t-t_0)]=A\,\delta(t-t_0)$.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Differentiate the unshifted step $u(t)$ to obtain the base impulse $\delta(t)$.
paragraph_plan: Introduce the idea that a derivative detects discontinuities in a signal and maps a unit step jump into an impulse form.
Write the base identity $\frac{d}{dt}u(t)=\delta(t)$ and define what this means in practice.
Generalize to a shifted step: $\frac{d}{dt}u(t-t_0)=\delta(t-t_0)$ and state how to read the jump location from the argument.
Finish with the scaled shifted form and point out linearity for upcoming examples.
